summary: Stuart Island Airstrip (YRR) is a small remote airstrip serving the community of Big Bay on Stuart Island, located off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, Canada. The airstrip provides a vital transportation link for residents and visitors to this isolated coastal community, which has no road access to the mainland. It primarily handles small charter and bush planes, supporting local residents, fishing lodges, and eco-tourism operations in the region.
faqs:
Q: Where is Stuart Island Airstrip located?
A: Stuart Island Airstrip is located on Stuart Island in British Columbia, Canada, serving the small community of Big Bay near the northern end of the island.

Q: Are there scheduled airline services at YRR?
A: No scheduled commercial airline service operates to Stuart Island Airstrip. The airport is primarily used for charter flights, private aviation, and air access for residents and visitors to the remote community.

Q: What is the best way to reach Stuart Island by air?
A: Charter flights from Campbell River or other Vancouver Island airports are the most common way to reach Stuart Island. Floatplane and small wheeled aircraft operators serve the area.

Q: Is the airstrip paved?
A: Stuart Island Airstrip is a small gravel or turf runway typical of remote British Columbia coastal airstrips, suited only for small bush planes and light aircraft.
transport_tips: As Stuart Island has no road connection to the mainland, air travel via charter aircraft is the primary means of reaching the airstrip. Visitors typically arrange flights from Campbell River or other Vancouver Island points, often through operators who also service the nearby Broughton Archipelago region. Boat access is an alternative, but weather conditions in the area can affect both sea and air travel, so flexibility in travel plans is recommended.
local_tip: Pack all essentials with you as the airstrip and Big Bay area have very limited supply services; the nearest stores and amenities require travel to larger Vancouver Island communities. Weather in the coastal waters can change quickly, so building buffer time into return flights is wise.
